implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy owns the token through mapper options: declare an integer version_id column (NOT NULL) and set __mapper_args__ = {'version_id_col': version_id}; the ORM then emits UPDATE ... WHERE id = :id AND version_id = :seen and raises sqlalchemy.orm.exc.StaleDataError when zero rows matched, deletes included. Django deliberately has no first-party counter, so its realization is manual: QuerySet.update() returns the number of rows matched, so Model.objects.filter(pk=..., version=seen).update(version=F('version') + 1, ...) returning 0 is the stale signal, and packages such as django-concurrency add the version field and its convention. Use the ORM-managed form for flushed unit-of-work writes; keep the filter-update when the framework has no counter or the statement is set-based.
code_sketch:
class Doc(Base):                       # SQLAlchemy 2.0
    __tablename__ = "doc"
    id = mapped_column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    version_id = mapped_column(Integer, nullable=False)
    body = mapped_column(Text)
    __mapper_args__ = {"version_id_col": version_id}

doc.body = new_body
session.commit()   # UPDATE ... WHERE id = :id AND version_id = :v
                   # zero rows -> StaleDataError (re-read, merge, retry)
pitfalls: Session.flush() is what performs the check: Query.update()/Query.delete() and raw SQL bypass the version counter entirely.
A NULL version column disables the comparison - SQLAlchemy documents the feature as not supporting NULL, so the column must be NOT NULL.
expire_on_commit=False reuses rows across transactions; without a refresh a later flush compares an old token and can raise StaleDataError against your own earlier commit.
Server-side counters (xmin, trigger-maintained columns) need RETURNING support, otherwise the ORM re-selects the value and re-opens the race it was trying to close.

variants.name: Django conditional update with rowcount test
variants.implementation_notes: Django has no built-in optimistic locking, so the token is application-owned: add an integer version field to the model, include the version you read in the filter of an update() call, set the new value with F('version') + 1 so the increment happens in the database, and treat the returned row count (the number of rows matched) of 0 as the stale signal. This keeps the check inside one UPDATE statement without any ORM feature, which is also why it survives across the framework's iterations, and third-party helpers simply package the same convention. The trade-off is that every write path must repeat the filter and the F() increment.
variants.code_sketch:
updated = (Doc.objects
    .filter(pk=doc_id, version=seen_version)
    .update(body=next_body, version=F('version') + 1))
if updated == 0:
    raise StaleCopyError        # re-read, merge or 409
# never Doc.save() here: it would overwrite without the check
pitfalls: Model.save() writes every field and carries no version predicate, so mixing it with the conditional update re-opens the lost update.
Filtering on a version that a concurrent transaction already changed is the expected path, not an error case - but the caller must not silently drop the user's edit without telling them.
